title: Trans Pregnancy Drama ‘Aman’ Boards Parallax Films for Global Sales Ahead of Toronto and London Premieres (EXCLUSIVE)
description: International sales company Parallax Films has boarded “Aman,” writer-director Rahul Roye’s short film about a trans man who discovers he is pregnan
body:
International sales company Parallax Films has boarded “Aman,” writer-director Rahul Roye’s short film about a trans man who discovers he is pregnant on the eve of his gender-affirming surgery, for worldwide sales. 

	The announcement comes ahead of the film’s world premiere in the Short Cuts competition at the Toronto Film Festival, after which it travels to the BFI London Film Festival for its European premiere in that festival’s competition section, which selects 10 shorts from across the world.
	

	Parallax Films is an international sales agent rooted in Sinophone cinema with teams based in Asia and Europe, focused on bringing high-quality Asian films to the global market. 


	Parallax founder Liuying Cao said: “‘Aman’ is an ambitious film, yet one deeply grounded in human emotion. It touches upon the most intimate experiences of an individual life, while never losing sight of the social and political realities – and responsibilities – that those experiences carry. Rather than resorting to slogans, the film reaches the audience through pain that is visceral, embodied, and deeply human. We are especially thrilled to be collaborating with such a beautiful and moving queer film from India.”

	The 16-minute film, a U.K.-U.S.-India-France co-production shot in the Hindi and Bengali languages, had previously unveiled Nikkhil Advani and Dominique Welinski as executive producers. It is produced by Apoorva Bakshi for Awedacious Originals, Elle León Nostas for Aymara Films, Neeraj Churi for Lotus Visual Productions, and Tushar Tyagi and Abid Aziz Merchant.

	The producers said in a joint statement: “‘Parallax Films brings a rare combination of global sales expertise and a deeply bespoke approach to every film they represent. With ‘Aman,’ we wanted a partner who could hold our sensitive and layered film with gentle hands, protecting what makes it intimate and singular while being ambitious and precise about how it is positioned for the world. Their instinct for both the film and its audience made the partnership feel immediate, and we’re thrilled to have them champion ‘Aman’ internationally.”
	

	The cast includes Kabir Maan, a transgender activist making his acting debut in the title role, opposite Sirat Taneja, Guntaj Deep Singh and Satakshi Nandy. Taneja previously appeared at Toronto in Deepa Mehta’s documentary “I Am Sirat.”

	“‘Aman’ is my attempt to create space for bodies and identities that refuse simplification. Pregnancy is one of the most deeply gendered experiences in our societies – ritualized, politicized and controlled. By placing a trans man at its center, the film questions how fragile our definitions of gender can be. Ultimately, it is a film about becoming,” Roye said.

	“Aman” is supported by the Sumitra Gupta Foundation for the Arts, the Keshav Suri Foundation and the Kashish Q Drishti Film Grant, presented by the Kashish Arts Foundation, with additional support from Renuka Shahane and Lotus Visual Productions. The film marks Roye’s third short, following “Man & Wife” and “A Lullaby for Yellow Roses.”

schema.headline: Trans Pregnancy Drama ‘Aman’ Boards Parallax Films for Global Sales Ahead of Toronto and London Premieres (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Oscars: Philippines Selects Rafael Manuel’s ‘Filipiñana’ for International Feature Race
description: Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana” has been chosen as the official entry from the Philippines in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Aw
body:
Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana” has been chosen as the official entry from the Philippines in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. It was selected from a shortlist of 8 films. 

	The film is written and directed by Manuel and is distributed by Kino Lorber.

	Richard Lorber, chair and CEO of Kino Lorber, said, “From the moment I saw ‘Filipiñana’ at the Sundance Film Festival, I’ve been telling everyone I know that it’s nothing short of a cinematic miracle.” He added, “When you’ve been distributing films for many decades, as I have, it feels like a gift that you can still discover something that truly feels like the future of the form. I am beyond thrilled that Rafael Manuel’s stunning and astounding debut has been chosen as the Philippines’ official Oscar submission and wish to reaffirm Kino Lorber’s commitment to helping it go the distance. ‘Filipiñana’ is already a theatrical hit in North America and our team is poised and ready to work with the film’s producers to translate our ongoing publicity and marketing efforts into a successful awards campaign.”
	

	The film is set against a backdrop of oppressive heat and drought. The narrative follows Isabel, a 17-year-old from the provinces of the Philippines, who gets a job at a prestigious golf resort.


	Speaking with Variety, Manuel said he felt the golf course was the perfect setting for the film to explore societal inequities in the country. With the very first courses established on American military bases, the local elite eventually took over, making the golf course a center of power.
	

	“When you think about it, it’s a good metaphor for the country in that it’s very large and situated on a very fertile plot of land that’s toiled on and worked on by so many people, but ultimately enjoyed and profited from by only a select few.” That, Manuel said, illustrates the class divide that has been so ingrained in the Philippines.

	The international feature selections can be found here.

schema.headline: Oscars: Philippines Selects Rafael Manuel’s ‘Filipiñana’ for International Feature Race

title: Mahershala Ali Finally Made His ‘Blade’ Film With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’
description:
Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali finally made their “Blade” movie.

	On Saturday night, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” made its world premiere
body:
Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali finally made their “Blade” movie.

	On Saturday night, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” made its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival before its theatrical release on Sept. 25. Tariq’s film centers on Latif (Ali), a devout Muslim hitman who, following the sudden death of his wife, goes on the run with his teenage daughter (Adia, a revelation), 10-year-old son (Jahleel Kamara) and newborn baby on the hunt for breast milk and after running afoul of not only his boss but also Hwan (an unrecognizable John Cho), the gun-toting leader of an anti-pornography Christian cult.
	

	And yes, Ali dispatches his enemies with a long blade.


	Tariq (“Mogul Mowgli”) was hired by Marvel Studios to direct “Blade” — with two-time Oscar winner Ali in the starring role — all the way back in 2021, but backed out of helming the project in 2022 due to production delays, staying on as an executive producer. The film was then stuck in development hell, and by July 2026, Ali confirmed it was dead in the water. So, Ali put the sword-fighting skills he’d learned training for the superhero to good use in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” a powerful meditation on religion, family and the ties that bind.

	Following its premiere, Tariq, Ali and the cast participated in a Q&A at the packed Princess of Wales Theatre.

	“It just all felt like the worlds were colliding all the time, every day and in every scene on that set,” Ali said of making the intense film. “Bassam gave us a lot to carry. I’m really grateful for the task and all the duties involved in playing this character. There’s something very special in working with my children in the film… The experience, the part, it’s all a bit of an emotional blur. And I’m still learning about it.”
	

	In addition to Ali’s magnetic performance, which deserves serious awards consideration, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” marks a breakout turn for Adia as his rebellious daughter struggling to balance her faith and teendom. And Adia had nothing but praise for her onscreen dad who she says allowed her to reach such great emotional depths.

	“Mahershala is such an incredibly generous soul in his scene work but also off camera,” Adia shared. “He really gave me the space to share myself off camera and on camera in a way that I’m not sure a lot of people get, so it made it a lot easier to approach the work — especially really tough scenes.”

	As for Ali’s fight scenes, he and Tariq gave a shout-out to Adam Hart, the film’s stunt coordinator, who choreographed the sequences in a short amount of time. “I’m so blown away with what he was able to choreograph and pull off within the time that we had,” said Ali. “It was a beautiful experience. Bassam and I met many years back, and I had had a year-plus of doing martial-arts training, and then I had over a year off of that. Bassam came to me with this incredible script and I had to do what I had to do and had my process in terms of getting to a yes. Once it was time to go, it just happened to be Ramadan and I was fasting and training a bit in L.A., and as soon as Ramadan was done, we started shooting.”

schema.headline: Mahershala Ali Finally Made His ‘Blade’ Film With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’

title: Paramount Leaving California Would Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds
description: A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Par
body:
A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Paramount Skydance out of California.

	A copy of the report published by Politico reads, “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031.”
	

	Reps for Paramount had no comment on the matter. 


	In August, news broke of Ellison’s plan to take Paramount Skydance out of the Golden State if California Attorney General Rob Bonta and a coalition of other state AGs did not come to the bargaining table and settle their lawsuit to stop the $111 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Ellison gave the AGs until Oct. 1, or he would start packing. The company is considering states such as Georgia, Texas and Tennessee.

	The report went on to outline some big-picture stats for if and when Paramount Skydance completed the move: “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output.”

	On Oct. 1, Paramount Skydance will have to start paying a “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders of $7 million a day until the deal closes. The trial between Ellison and the AGs is scheduled to start on March 2, meaning that without a settlement, Paramount is on the hook for about $1.3 billion to WBD shareholders.
	

	In late August, progress toward a settlement seemed promising after Bonta and Ellison scheduled a meeting on Aug. 24. In a last-minute move, Bonta canceled the meeting, accusing the Paramount camp of leaking details of their discussions. Paramount denied the accusations, but Bonta did not relent, saying in a statement he won’t return to settlement talks until they put a “lid on their lying leaks.”

schema.headline: Paramount Leaving California Would Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds

title: ‘Animal Hospital’ Leads Roblox Innovation Awards 2026 Winners as Roblox Unveils 20th Anniversary Event
description: The Roblox Innovation Awards (RIAs) unveiled its 2026 winners during a ceremony in San Jose Saturday with new title “Animal Hospital” taking home se
body:
The Roblox Innovation Awards (RIAs) unveiled its 2026 winners during a ceremony in San Jose Saturday with new title “Animal Hospital” taking home several top honors.

	Part of the 12th annual Roblox Developer Conference, this year’s RIAs were hosted by Roblox’s head of the developer community, Justin Sousa (widely known as “JParty” to Roblox users).

	The RIAs honor Roblox developers, artists, studios and creators across 20 categories. This years results were calculated based on 319 million votes.
	

	“What I love most about this list is how different all of these winners are,” Sousa said. “There isn’t one definition of a great Roblox game anymore, and that’s the point. From tactical shooters and terrifying forests to word games, football, fashion, audio, and one particularly suspicious medical facility, the boundaries of what can be built on Roblox keep moving because this community keeps moving them.”


	The RIAs were held at the conclusion of this year’s Roblox Developers Conference, during which Roblox made several big announcements, including the reveal of Roblox’s upcoming 20th anniversary event, “The Hunt.”

	Per Sousa, “Roblox has been around for two decades now, and it shows in the breadth of ingenuity creators bring to the table. For those who missed the RIAs live, we also announced a special event to celebrate Roblox’s 20-year anniversary, beginning on September 17—The Hunt: Roblox 20. But more on that later.”

	See below for the full list of winners announced during the 2026 Roblox Innovation Awards.
	
		Best Shooter	

	Game: RIVALSStudio: Nosniy GamesA polished, competitive FPS built around intense 1v1 duels to 5v5 battles. RIVALS is easy to jump into and very hard to put down.
	
	
		Best Use of Audio	

	Game: DOORSStudio: LSPLASHIn DOORS, sound isn’t just atmosphere—it’s part of how players understand the world, anticipate what’s coming, and occasionally realize they’re in serious trouble.
	
		Best Plugin	

	Plugin: UGC Makers ToolboxCreator: OnogorkA creator-built toolbox designed to make the process of building UGC easier. This is exactly the kind of thing we love seeing developers build for other developers.
	
		Best Puzzle Game	

	Game: Finish The WordStudio: Table Game XA wonderfully simple idea with surprisingly stressful consequences: Keep the word chain alive, think fast, and don’t be the one who runs out of answers.
	
		Best Innovation in a Branded Game	

	Partnership: Steal a Brainrot x GOAT (Sony Pictures)Studio: Do BigA collision of one of Roblox’s biggest cultural phenomena with a major entertainment property in a way that feels native to the experience rather than bolted onto it.
	
		Best Party & Casual Game	

	Game: +1 Speed Keyboard EscapeStudio: SecretVerse StudioLet’s chill … or maybe not? Fast, accessible, and delightfully chaotic, this is the kind of game where “one more round” can quickly turn into 10.
	
		Best Innovation in Tech	

	Game: TTKStudio: Sable DigitalAn ambitious tactical shooter pushing on what high-fidelity combat can look and feel like on Roblox, from helmet cams and optics to sophisticated squad-based gameplay.
	
		Best Sports Game	

	Game: FIFA Super SoccerStudio: Play! FootballFootball? Soccer? Who cares! FIFA Super Soccer brings the game’s energy, competition, and global appeal to Roblox.
	
		Best Action Game	

	Game: Jujutsu ShenanigansStudio: Tze’s ShenanigansFast combat, big abilities, destructive chaos, and exactly the right amount of shenanigans.
	
		Best UGC Creator	

	Creator: ValkenheimA creator whose distinctive work continues to show just how much personality and imagination can fit into an avatar.
	
		Best Innovation in Creative Direction	

	Game: Animal HospitalStudio: Animal AnomalyFrom the creepy hospital setting to the decidedly abnormal patients, Animal Hospital’s creative identity captures players’ attention almost immediately.
	
		Best Survival Game	

	Game: 99 Nights in the ForestStudio: Grandma’s Favourite GamesBuild a camp, gather resources, and rescue the missing kids. Survive this fantastic party game and stop whatever is watching from the forest over 99 very long nights.
	
	
		Best Strategy Game	

	Game: Mini WarStudio: M&M CommunityStart with a small country, build its economy, raise an army, and decide whether diplomacy or total domination is the better path to victory.
	
		Best RPG	

	Game: Piggy: IntercityStudio: Piggy: IntercityPiggy goes open world with exploration, characters, base building, and player choices that shape a journey through an infected world.
	
		Best Classic Game	

	Game: Natural Disaster SurvivalStudio: StickmasterlukeSurvive the flood, dodge the meteors, and stare in awe at the ones who make it through. Some Roblox lessons are timeless.
	
		Best Video Star	

	Video Star: Laughability (YouTube)Being a star has its perks. Thanks for the stories, humor, and unique creator-driven PoV!
	
		Best New Game	

	Game: Animal HospitalStudio: Animal AnomalyThe night shift at this animal hospital gets weird fast. Animal Hospital is a wonderfully unsettling mix of treating patients, spotting anomalies, and trying to survive until morning.
	
		People’s Choice	

	Game: Animal HospitalStudio: Animal AnomalyApparently the community agrees: Questionable veterinary practices make for a pretty great Roblox game.
	
		Best Studio	

	Studio: Nosniy Games

	A studio that continues to combine craft, polish, and a deep understanding of what makes players want to come back for one more game. Developers of games like Treasure Quest, Super Golf, and, of course, RIVALS, named this year’s Best Shooter. Also some pretty cool d00ds.
	
		The Builderman Award	

	Game: Animal HospitalStudio: Animal AnomalyAnd the final award goes to Animal Hospital, where working the night shift gets weird … fast.

schema.headline: ‘Animal Hospital’ Leads Roblox Innovation Awards 2026 Winners as Roblox Unveils 20th Anniversary Event

title: FCC Chairman Slams James Talarico as Running a ‘Hoax’ With Jimmy Kimmel Interview, Which ABC Punted to YouTube, to Get ‘Clicks and Donations’
description: Brendan Carr, the Trump-aligned Republican chairman of the FCC, accused James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, of running a “
body:
Brendan Carr, the Trump-aligned Republican chairman of the FCC, accused James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, of running a “hoax” to garner attention and campaign donations by sitting for an interview with Jimmy Kimmel — which ABC put on YouTube instead airing it on broadcast TV to avoid a potential clash with the FCC.

	In a post on X Saturday night, Carr wrote that Talarico is “just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations — he’s banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings.”
	

	Carr’s post included a meme mocking Talarico and Kimmel meant to show a self-inflicted fail. It depicts Kimmel riding a bike with Talarico tucked into a baby backpack carrier on the TV host’s shoulders; Kimmel then inserts a stick into the spokes, causing the bike to crash.


	Variety has reached out to Talarico’s press office for comment.

	Kimmel on Wednesday announced on his ABC late-night show that the interview Talarico would be on YouTube and not TV, saying the decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense.”

	The concern was that the FCC would retaliate against ABC over Talarico’s appearance under the agency’s equal-time rule, which requires broadcast programs give equivalent airtime to political candidates (unless they are “bona fide” news programs). Late-night shows and daytime talk shows have long been considered exempt from the rule. But earlier this year, Carr kicked off a formal review of whether ABC daytime talk show “The View” qualifies for an exemption to the equal-time rule. The FCC chairman has alleged that many talk shows on broadcast networks function as partisan mouthpieces for Democrats and should be subject to agency regulations like the equal-time rule and a prohibition on “news distortion,” because they are using publicly licensed TV spectrum.
	

	Talarico characterized ABC’s decision to abstain from putting his interview with Kimmel on TV as effectively amounting to censorship by the U.S. government. “Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” Talarico said in an interview Thursday on MS NOW. The Democrat called the FCC’s threats against broadcasters over “The View” and other programming “the most dangerous form of cancel culture.”

	After Kimmel’s interview with Talarico was posted Thursday on YouTube, it notched over 5 million views in the first 24 hours. As of this writing, it has racked up 7.3 million views on the platform.

	“We are being targeted by the FCC for the crime of interviewing political candidates,” Kimmel said at the top of the segment. “Even though, for years, we and every other late-night talk show have welcomed numerous candidates including Donald Trump when he was running [for president]. He was on this show two times. But now I guess he doesn’t like me anymore or the First Amendment. And so the FCC has threatened me or threatened my show, our network, even our local ABC stations because they want to make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept. And so tonight, we are bypassing the public airwaves and hosting this interview on YouTube, even though our government would clearly prefer that we not do it at all.”

	Earlier this year, Talarico similarly was kept off TV over CBS’s fear of running afoul of Carr’s enforcement of the FCC equal time rule. In February, Stephen Colbert said CBS execs pulled his interview with Talarico from air over concerns about violating the equal time rule. CBS said it didn’t block the interview from airing but that the network provided “The Late Show” producers “legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule.”

	Meanwhile, ABC has dragged the FCC into federal court over the agency’s demand it submit licenses for its eight owned-and-operated TV stations early renewal. ABC sued the FCC and Carr last month, alleging the commission was waging an “extraordinary assault” on its First Amendment rights through the implicit threat of revoking its local TV broadcast. The Disney-owned broadcaster’s lawsuit alleged that the FCC’s “true target” is not the stations’ employment practices but the content of their programming: “Because the Commission cannot regulate that content directly, it has used its review of the Stations’ licenses as an instrument to the same end,” the suit said. The FCC asserts the ABC early license renewal was initiated from the agency’s investigation into “allegations of unlawful discrimination” in employment practices at Disney and ABC. On Sept. 3, the agency asked the court to dismiss ABC’s lawsuit, arguing that the network failed to establish that the license review represents “retaliation” for disfavored speech.
	

	Carr, in his Saturday-night commentary, was responding to a comment on X by an organization called University Democrats at UT Austin, which asked rhetorically, “So I can’t watch Talarico on Kimmel but I have to watch Ted Cruz on GameDay?” That’s a reference to an appearance on ESPN’s “College GameDay” Saturday by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who was on-air for almost 10 minutes. Cruz, who spent most of his time on the program lobbying for the Protect College Sports Act legislation that would impose new restrictions on collegiate sports practices, was loudly heckled and booed by the fans in attendance.

	Carr, who was appointed chairman of the FCC by Donald Trump in 2025, noted that the FCC’s equal-time rule doesn’t apply to ESPN’s “College GameDay” because Congress applied it to broadcast TV stations, not cable networks. In addition, he pointed out correctly, the statute only applies to “legally qualified candidates” running for office.

	He also argued that the equal-time statute “does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast tv. It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others.”

	Carr, explaining why broadcast and cable networks are regulated differently by the FCC, continued, “Broadcasters are unique. The FCC gave them free licenses worth many billions of dollars to use a public resource (spectrum). They are given a government sanctioned monopoly on their broadcast frequencies, too. If anyone else wants to use that same public resource (spectrum) for the purpose of expressing their own views, the government will not let them — it will eject anyone else that tries to use a broadcaster’s licensed spectrum.”

	The Supreme Court has ruled that “holding broadcasters to their public interest obligations is not censorship or any sort of 1A [First Amendment] violation,” Carr wrote. “And Congress has charged the FCC with ensuring that broadcasters meet those public interest obligations, as required by their licenses. The agency should do so.”

	Of course, today, most Americans watch broadcast television networks like ABC on cable, satellite or internet pay-TV services — not using over-the-air antennas.
	

	In response to Carr’s 479-word post, UT Austin’s University Democrats wrote, “ok brandon.”

schema.headline: FCC Chairman Slams James Talarico as Running a ‘Hoax’ With Jimmy Kimmel Interview, Which ABC Punted to YouTube, to Get ‘Clicks and Donations’

title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Chris Rock Tells the Story of a Party-Girl Actress, Brilliantly Played by Rosalind Eleazar, in The Best Movie About Hollywood in Years
description: The title character of “Misty Green,” Chris Rock’s explosively entertaining, savagely authentic drama about life in the Hollywood of today, is a tel
body:
The title character of “Misty Green,” Chris Rock’s explosively entertaining, savagely authentic drama about life in the Hollywood of today, is a television actress who had a moment — in fact, she was close to the top of the heap. But that was then and this is now. Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar (“Slow Horses”) with doleful charisma and a casual fury, is in her late 30s. She’s a vivid and acclaimed actress and singer who was popular enough to have won the Emmy for best supporting actress for her cult thriller series “Red Eye.” She was on the cover of Cosmo. People still talk about her show in reverent tones.
	

	Yet it’s funny how time passes. At an audition, Misty is seated next to a young actress who’s awed to meet her, because “Red Eye” was her mother’s favorite show. Misty still has her looks, her talent, and her drive (everything you need, right?). And she’s still out there working it. But her career has been in a slump, and that kind of downhill mojo can take on a life of its own. Suddenly you look up and you’re a has-been. 


	It doesn’t help that Misty is an unapologetic party girl. She likes to drink, drug, and fuck whoever to the point that it’s getting more than a bit self-destructive. The night before that audition, she gets a text from Zack (Adam Driver), an oily tech power-player sleazebag who always has a harem of women around him, which he maintains by keeping them well-supplied with cocaine. Misty hooks up with him for a night of clubbing, snorting, and screwing in the bathroom stall, and the next morning she’s a wreck. But her hellbent hedonism, and the recklessness that grows out of what’s really an orgiastic form of self-medicating, didn’t happen by accident.
	

	Misty is pissed off. The big picture of her career is that the industry, because of its values (and because of her defiant nature, though that’s the very quality that made her a star), is slowly but surely choking off her options. She’s Black, which is no deal-killer but still, in the eyes of too many, puts her in a box. She’s getting “old.” And she has slept around enough, and acted thoughtlessly enough, flying off the handle, that she has left a trail of enemies. There are too many people who look at her and think she’s trouble. In the new corporate Hollywood run by algorithm, trouble means not fitting into the machine. At the same time, Misty has been at the game for so long that she’s become a round-the-clock liar. She deceives and manipulates to survive, and that’s part of her performance vibe — she’s always acting. She’s a star, a diva, and a mess.

	Last year, a lot of people clutched pearls over whether the title character of “Marty Supreme” was “likable” enough. Misty Green makes Marty look like an Eagle Scout. The movie, however, isn’t apologizing for its heroine’s bad behavior or making excuses for her. She has made her own bed. What’s mesmerizing about “Misty Green” is that Misty is part of an entertainment industry that has cut so many corners, and has so many pathologies, that it’s hard to separate the corruption she’s up against from her own self-inflicted damage. As a filmmaker, Chris Rock wants us to know Misty as if we were in her skin (he has cited the films of John Cassavetes, like “A Woman Under the Influence,” as one of his role models). At the same time, “Misty Green” is an amazing slice of showbiz sociology, riveting in the details of what a contemporary Hollywood actress — even a successful one — is up against. Rock isn’t casting stones. The warped values he depicts are there in the industry and in Misty herself.

	In the eyebrow-raiser of an opening scene, we meet Misty in the fabulous beachfront apartment she’s been living in for four years. It belongs to the wealthy player she was the mistress of, who has just died; his wife walks in in a rage and demands that Misty leave. But then she recognizes Misty (like everyone, she was a fan of “Red Eye”), which provokes a suddenly sympathetic reaction. She’ll let Misty stay in the apartment for one more week. This scene, with its machine-gun insults and effusive obscenity, establishes several key things: that Hollywood is a place where people like Misty let themselves be used; that it’s a place that will toss you out; and that the sway of celebrity may be fickle, but it’s still all-powerful.
	

	Misty is broke, without a home, and without too many prospects. (That audition is for a “street” role — in other words, what a Black actress is expected to do.) Yet she’s still Misty Green! And the movie, set against the ticking countdown clock of that week, uses Misty’s crisis of survival to take a spiritual inventory of Hollywood.

	I knew it when I saw “Top Five,” the last movie he directed (12 years ago!), but now it can be shouted from the rooftops: Chris Rock is a major filmmaker. He is, of course, flexing different muscles here than he is as a stand-up comedian, but part of his delicious gift as a writer-director is that he draws on the extraordinary empirical powers that drive his stand-up. Like all the greatest comedians, he’s really a philosopher-detective, and the beauty of “Misty Green” is that it’s not some stylized “satire” of the new entertainment culture. The movie has laughs, a lot of them dark, but Rock has insisted that people call it a drama, and I get why he’s touchy on the point. The lure of “Misty Green” is its authenticity.

	You feel that in your bones when Misty goes into the audition, and there at the table is Rhonda (Tracie Thoms), the veteran casting director who’s known her for so long that she can’t see who Misty is anymore. (A rival actress praises Misty to the heavens, all as a sly way of putting her down.) You feel it when Misty is dishing with her best friend, Naomi (Anna Kendrick), an actress who’s getting out of the business by marrying a finance dude (Rich Sommer) she’s far from in love with — and, in fact, she still yearns for random erotic encounters. But if that sounds chortle-worthy, it’s really expressive of the L.A. state-of-mind of the “Real Housewives” era, where everything is transactional. And you feel it in Misty’s encounters with Zach the demon of temptation, who’s both lover and pimp — one of those character roles that Adam Driver, with his quick-hit hustler’s aggression, is perfect for. Zack offers Misty 200 grand to go to Dubai and party with the royalty there. He’s asking her to prostitute herself, but the point is that Zack – and Dubai — is now part of the Hollywood chain.     

	Rock has cast himself in the movie as well. Acting with a jovial diffidence, wearing a porkpie hat he never takes off, he plays Jordan Green, a film director Missy once worked with (on an update of “Cinderella”), until she came in one day so high on coke that she punched a crew member. So Jordan is another burnt bridge, except that Rock, an infectious presence (even if he isn’t quite an actor), invests him with empathy and gives him a lot of fun lines (like his explanation of why “all Civil Rights movies suck”). Rock, with his scolding amusement, is there, in a way, to expound on the subtle racism of latter-day Hollywood, and to give Misty a break because of it. Jordan is directing a reboot of “Dreamgirls,” to be shot in Vancouver, and maybe this could be Misty’s second chance.
	

	The other major character is Misty’s brother (also named Jordan), who is bipolar and turns violent whenever he goes off his meds. He’s played by Daniel Kaluuya, in his first screen performance in four years, and Kaluuya is a force. When Jordan erupts at a waiter for not bringing the bill to him, we see that his mental illness carries an echo of Nina Simone’s “irrational” rage. She was bipolar too, but this, the movie says, is the mad despair that a sensitivity to entrenched racism can drive you to. And Misty’s loyalty to her brother — to that side of him — is part of her undoing.

	Yet Misty still has the goods. At the Roosevelt Hotel cabaret, she does a performance of Radiohead’s “Creep,” and it’s hypnotic. “Dreamgirls” would be perfect for her, and she and Jordan know it. Rosalind Eleazar shows us Misty’s duplicity, but she acts with such unguarded emotion that we’re desperate to see her burn through her problems and succeed. When she finally does her “Dreamgirls” audition, and sings “One Night Only,” it carries the film’s payload of hope and despair. Chris Rock is right: This is a drama. Yet “Misty Green” is put together with so much observational exuberance that it leaves you both daunted and exhilarated.

schema.headline: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Chris Rock Tells the Story of a Party-Girl Actress, Brilliantly Played by Rosalind Eleazar, in The Best Movie About Hollywood in Years

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Anthony Ippolito Channels Sylvester Stallone in Peter Farrelly’s Cleverly Crafted Crowd-Pleaser About the Making of ‘Rocky’
description: For a biographical drama to work, it’s not required that the central actor do a pinpoint uncanny, so-close-to- the-real-thing-you-might-think-it’s-t
body:
For a biographical drama to work, it’s not required that the central actor do a pinpoint uncanny, so-close-to- the-real-thing-you-might-think-it’s-the-real-thing impersonation of the person he’s playing. But Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” may be a special case. It’s a movie about the making of “Rocky” — about how Sylvester Stallone, then a two-bit actor in his late 20s, dreamed it, wrote it, sold it, and insisted he play the lead role in it. Since “Rocky” is one of the most popular and beloved movies ever made, and Stallone one of the most famous stars in the history of Hollywood, it’s actually essential for the actor playing him to get it right. If not, we would just be in cheesy-tacky TV-movie land.
	

	Anthony Ippolito, who plays Sylvester Stallone in “I Play Rocky,” gets it just right. He looks startlingly like Stallone: the droopy dark eyes, the slightly jutting lips with the delicate dip at the center, even the skin tone — that sort of peach-ivory pallor. And Ippolito’s impersonation of Stallone’s voice is a miraculous act of channeling. He gets that super-low back-of-the-throat growl, the mush-mouth intonation, the words dripping out like molasses, the sense that his whole personality is a slow-motion amiable grumble. Watching and listening to Anthony Ippolito, we can believe that Sylvester Stallone is standing right in front of us, though the performance is more than just an awesome impersonation. He’s truly playing Stallone —  the sweetly stubborn and dogged person he was at the time.


	“I Play Rocky” is a cleverly crafted crowd-pleaser, all designed to tap into the love of “Rocky” that has never gone away (this November it will be 50 years since “Rocky” was released). But in a funny way I found the film to have a surprising spirit in common with “Nouvelle Vague,” Richard Linklater’s 2025 drama about the making of Jean-Luc Godard’s “Breathless.” Linklater’s film was also a rich piece of nostalgia (the high-end black-and-white cinephile version). And what made it work, apart from the sheer meticulous authenticity with which Linklater recreated the shooting of “Breathless” in the streets and hotels and cafés of Paris, was that Linklater captured the revolutionary form-follows-function dimension of what made “Breathless” a great movie — the fact that Godard made it up as he went along, and how that radical spontaneity found its way into the DNA of the film.
	

	The story told by “I Play Rocky” isn’t so different. As written by Peter Gamble, the film opens in New York City in 1974, when Stallone is living in a Times Square fleabag, doing all he can to get acting jobs, though it’s not going anywhere. All he gets offered are roles like “Thug #2” (which he tries out for in the opening scene). He has no money and gets kicked out of the flophouse, where he meets a homeless pug who becomes his pet. He’s so down-and-out he’s reduced to trying out for a soft-core porn film (Stallone was actually in one, though that was back in 1970).

	The first thing that saves him is meeting Sasha, the ticket-seller at the movie theater he gets a job at. They become a couple, and she’s the one who tells him that if he isn’t getting the parts he wants, maybe he should write a script that features the kind of role he’d like to do. Sasha is played by AnnaSophia Robb, who makes her supportive in a spiky way that had me thinking of another ’70s icon — she sounds like she’s channeling Karen Lynn Gorney from “Saturday Night Fever.” (Could the making of that one be the sequel?)

	Sly and Sasha get married and move to Los Angeles, where Stallone finds work as a parking attendant, and he keeps writing scripts. But lightning doesn’t strike until March 24, 1975, when he settles into a bar to have a beer and, on television, starts to watch the championship match between Muhammad Ali and the aging underdog Chuck Wepner. The match is a set-up — the chance for Ali to knock out his opponent in two or three rounds. But instead, Wepner goes the distance, and even gets in a few major licks. He’s standing, against all odds, after 15 rounds, and that triggers something in Stallone. (Stallone has claimed that he was not inspired to make “Rocky” by that match. But clearly the filmmakers decided to ignore him.)

	Stallone has already met with the producing team of Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Tony Kebbell), who constitute a major eruption of ugly geek clothing and bad ’70 hair, and they like his script for “Paradise Alley.” But then he shows them the script for “Rocky.” They read it and love it; it’s got something. They want to make the film, and after meeting with Sandy Maddox (Tracy Letts), an amusingly blustery-for-the-time-but-now-rather-quaint-seeming studio suit (he’s a fictional composite of several movie executives of the era), they agree to pay Stallone $50,000 for his script, which means that he’ll be off and running. There’s just one problem. As Stallone puts it, “I play Rocky.” That, for him, is the dream and the deal. It’s the only option.
	

	For a while, “I Play Rocky” is a high comedy of negotiation, as Winkler and Chartoff, who have secured a relatively low budget of $2 million to make “Rocky,” keep offering Stallone more and more money for his script, and he keeps turning them down. They go as high as $350,000 (a lot of money for 1975). But Stallone’s need to play Rocky is non-negotiable, and the essence of that whim of iron is that it’s the true-life version of Rocky Balboa’s need to be a contender. The pleasure of “I Play Rocky” is that it understands the karmic way in which the story of “Rocky” — the underdog who triumphs against all odds — was echoed in the saga of how Stallone got the movie off the ground.

	The making of “Rocky,” which was compellingly chronicled in the 2023 documentary “Sly,” has an epic irony built into it: the fact that Stallone created one of the most iconic characters in movie history, yet you can absolutely understand why the powers that be at the time didn’t want him to star in the movie. He was a total unknown (they wanted a movie star), but more than that he was an actor who looked half-asleep and sounded like he had a dozen frogs in his throat. Who in his right mind would greenlight that?

	But that’s where the story becomes rich. Stallone has Winkler and Chartoff over a barrel; they can’t make the movie without him. And so, worn down at last, they agree to let him star in “Rocky,” but they only have the contractual right to do so if they reduce the budget to $1 million. Which is peanuts. But that becomes integral to how “Rocky” turned into a great movie.

	The director they hire, John G. Avildsen (played with hackish exuberance by Jay Duplass), is known for working fast and cheap, but the budget for “Rocky” is so low that he’s going to have to outdo himself. They decide to set the movie in Philadelphia, so that they can shoot it without unions. They’ll use the newly developed Steadicam to glide up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Stallone will pull tendons and bust knuckles punching the overly frozen meat slabs in the lockers, but he won’t be allowed to heal for even one day, because if they fall behind then Sandy Maddox has the right to fire Stallone (which is what he wants to do). Did I mention that neither Stallone nor his co-star Carl Weathers (Stephan James) have the slightest idea of how to box? The production hires a legendary Hollywood boxing choreographer (Trevor St. John), who has staged 14 classic fight movies, but Stallone thinks they all look the same. He wants his own version of realism. And so he and Weathers will figure out how to punch each other.
	

	All of this makes “I Play Rocky” into a high comedy of Hollywood creativity. It’s about the making of one of the biggest mainstream hits of all time, but what it captures is that “Rocky” wasn’t just a ’70s movie; it was a catch-as-catch-can shoestring fluke. (When the producers first play a tape of Bill Conte’s famous theme music, Winkler says it’s ways too “grandiose.”) And Stallone really did bring his own life into it. The scene where he rages away at Burgess Meredith’s Mickey, retro-fitting Marlon Brando’s “I coulda been a contender” speech, is Hollywood magic, because Stallone draws it out of himself. (He’s really railing at his a-hole father, played in the movie by Matt Dillon.) Almost every aspect of how “Rocky” was made taps into a desire to see movies echo reality.

	“I Play Rocky” has some of the slyness of movies-about-real-moviemaking that include “Nouvelle Vague” and “Baadasssss!” and — the “Citizen Kane” of the genre — “Ed Wood.” But as infectious as the film is, there’s one thing that “I Play Rocky” takes so much for granted it doesn’t quite dramatize it: the way that “Rocky” wasn’t just a great movie — a Frank Capra fable dusted in ’70s grit — but a movie that changed America. The New Hollywood was desolate and dark. “Star Wars” is the film that’s generally credited for remaking movie culture, but it was actually “Rocky,” with its new-style old-school optimism, that did that. More than any other film, it kicked open the door to the Reagan revolution by rekindling our primal need for happy endings. Stallone played Rocky. But he really played all of our desire to return to belief. Wherever that might lead.

schema.headline: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Anthony Ippolito Channels Sylvester Stallone in Peter Farrelly’s Cleverly Crafted Crowd-Pleaser About the Making of ‘Rocky’

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Premieres at TIFF: A Movie About a Best Picture Winner That’s a Best Picture Contender?
description:
Yo Adrian, Rocky did it … again!

	Only this time, the famed character is at TIFF in biopic form, thanks to director Peter Farrelly, screenwriter Pe
body:
Yo Adrian, Rocky did it … again!

	Only this time, the famed character is at TIFF in biopic form, thanks to director Peter Farrelly, screenwriter Peter Gamble and a star-making turn from Anthony Ippolito, who portrays actor Sylvester Stallone in the story of his relentless determination to bring “Rocky” to the big screen. This has the DNA of a TIFF Audience winner through and through.


	“I Play Rocky” held its world premiere Saturday night as part of the festival’s Special Presentations program at the Princess of Wales Theatre. It’s one of the very first movies that has played at the festival that has the potential to win TIFF’s highest honor — the People’s Choice Award. Multiple applauses rang throughout the film as the film recreates the highest points of the 1976 MGM flick that became the highest grossing movie of its respective year, went on to be nominated for 10 Oscars, and winning three including best picture. A post-screening Q&A with Farelly, Ipplolito, Stephan James, Jay Duplass and screenwriter Peter Gamble.
	



	

					“I Play Rocky”
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	There’s a certain symmetry in watching a movie about an unknown who bet everything on himself arrive at the very festival that once turned a modest crowd-pleaser into a best picture winner. Farrelly knows that route. Eight years ago, “Green Book” won the TIFF People’s Choice Award and marched all the way to a best picture statuette. Now the director returns to TIFF with “I Play Rocky,” the story of how a broke, stubborn Sylvester Stallone talked Hollywood into letting him write and star in “Rocky.” 
	

	The film chronicles one of Hollywood’s most improbable success stories: a struggling actor with a script nobody wanted and one nonnegotiable demand — that he play the lead himself. As studios dangle money on the condition that an established star throw the punches, Stallone digs in, turning the standoff that follows into its own kind of prizefight.

	The film’s origin, Farrelly told the Princess of Wales crowd, came down to a script and a self-tape. “I read this script and I thought it was the greatest script I’d ever read,” he said of Peter Gamble’s screenplay, before recounting how the search for his Stallone ended almost before it began. The director said his casting agent called one day claiming to have found the lead — a then-unknown Anthony Ippolito, who had gotten hold of the script and shot three scenes himself in his grandmother’s basement. “I looked at it and the search was over,” Farrelly said. “That’s the guy. We didn’t have to go any further.”

	If the casting feels like fate, that’s because it more or less is. Ippolito, a 27-year-old Long Island native who has been working since childhood, broke out as George Wright in the Netflix drama series “Grand Army” in 2020. He followed with a turn as a young Al Pacino in the Paramount+ limited series “The Offer,” about the making of “The Godfather.” That makes “I Play Rocky” the second time he has played a young Italian American icon at the dawn of a best picture winner — a coincidence too neat to ignore. Make no mistake: a star is born. Ippolito delivers the kind of breakout that turns a working actor into a name overnight, anchoring one of the truest underdog stories the business has ever told. 

	For Ippolito, stepping into the role meant a transformation that stretched across years, not months. “It took a lot of effort, upwards of a year and a half to two years,” the actor told the crowd, thanking Farrelly and the team for the gamble. “I’m just so grateful that they were willing to take a chance on me in this situation.” Then, taking in the room: “This is absolutely surreal.”

	The film carries the same magic and fervor as the 1976 original, and it stands as Peter Farrelly’s finest outing behind the camera — a triumph that plays as both a People’s Choice contender and a genuine Oscar threat. Film Twitter has made its position on Farrelly clear, and the knives will be out again, but that crowd has never been the point. This one is right up the Academy’s alley. The bench is deep, too. AnnaSophia Robb is quietly devastating as Sasha Czack, Stallone’s first wife and earliest believer, while Matt Dillon plays Frank Stallone Sr. Stephan James steps into the trunks as Carl Weathers, the actor who would become Apollo Creed, and Kiki Seto plays Talia Shire opposite Robert Morgan’s Burgess Meredith and Scot Teller’s Burt Young. Jay Duplass rounds out the group as “Rocky” director John G. Avildsen, with P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff — Byrne proving yet again what a formidable character actor he is, his Winkler nothing short of sublime.
	

	“I Play Rocky” premiered Sept. 12 at the Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios opens the film in limited release Nov. 6, expanding nationwide Nov. 20.

title: Chris Rock’s Hollywood Send-Up ‘Misty Green’ Hits TIFF With Rosalind Eleazar’s Knockout Lead Performance
description: Roughly two-thirds through “Misty Green,” Rosalind Eleazar takes a breath and lets a rendition of “One Night Only,” from the musical “Dreamgirls,” r
body:
Roughly two-thirds through “Misty Green,” Rosalind Eleazar takes a breath and lets a rendition of “One Night Only,” from the musical “Dreamgirls,” rip. The characters around her go quiet, and the crowd at the Toronto International Film Festival, where Chris Rock‘s film made its world premiere, seemed similarly enraptured.

	But when Rock and his cast took the stage for their post-screening Q&A, the crowd made their appreciation for her work known with cheers and applause.
	

	Onstage, Eleazar explained why she fell in love with Misty and was “really desperate” to play the part. 


	“It was such a raw and honest take on the darker side of our industry,” Eleazar said about reading the script for the first time (and charming the crowd with her British accent). “She’s such a complex and such a contradictory and flawed character, and I’m sort of drawn to characters that are difficult to love, and the way that Chris wrote the individual relationships with such precision and nuance.”

	“The moment I read the script in London, I was desperate to do this part. So I did whatever I could,” Eleazar said, before realizing what she’d accidentally insinuated, since Misty Green will indeed do anything for a role. Rock and the crowd chuckled as she hastily recovered: “Normal things! Just like Zooms and stuff.”

	Eleazar — recently named one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch for 2026 — is a best actress contender that dares anyone in the room to argue otherwise. Each scene feels fit for her Oscar clip package, much Cate Blanchett delivered in each beat of “Blue Jasmine.” Misty is a fading, award-winning actress clawing back her career, but self-sabotaging along the way. Eleazar plays her with the danger of Pam Grier and the polish of Tracee Ellis Ross.
	

	”I love a messy woman,” Rock said, explaining why he crafted the complex character in the first place. “I like to make things I haven’t seen: I haven’t seen it with a woman, I haven’t seen it with a Black woman.”

	As Rock explained in his Variety cover story, the role was a tricky one to cast because of its risqué nature, but Eleazar was game as could be.

	“I know she’s a lovely lady and demure tonight, but you have these meetings, and you have to think to yourself: ‘OK, is she gonna smoke the cigarette in her underwear on the balcony? Is she gonna get on the floor and fight for the money? Like on the day you can just say you’re not doing it, and what the fuck am I gonna do?”

	With “Misty Green,” Rock, who wrote and directed the film, crafted a dramatic satire that cuts to the bone. The film functions as a tour of Los Angeles’ most potable artistic hot spots, but doubles as an autopsy of the business, especially for artists of color. He skewers “Hollywood” without ever quite naming names. “Call Kevin,” one actor barks. “Is it Hart?” The film keeps daring you to fill in the blanks.

	Most importantly, Rock hands Eleazar showcase after showcase, and she cashes in on every opportunity. A sequence built around a screen test for “The Devil Wears Prada” is the funniest, sharpest stretch of acting in the film — until the next one that follows it. When Misty sings a version of Radiohead’s “Creep” in the lounge at the Hollywood Roosevelt, the ache lands similarly to Carey Mulligan’s “New York, New York” solo in “Shame.” By the time Eleazar reaches “One Night Only,” it’s her “La La Land” audition moment.

	Now, for the Oscar-shaped elephant in the room. Only one Black woman has won the lead actress Oscar: Halle Berry, for “Monster’s Ball,” in 2002. Now, 24 ceremonies later, could Eleazar be the most credible candidate to become the second? She’s more than worthy.

	And then there’s Daniel Kaluuya. The “Judas and the Black Messiah” Oscar winner has been away from screens for too long, and “Misty Green” is the argument for why the business can’t afford to keep letting that happen. He plays Misty’s brother, who grapples with his mental health. A single scene near the finale is enough to shatter your heart.
	

	Adam Driver turns up for a stretch that is, improbably, the best thing he does all year — better even than his work in “Paper Tiger” — as a Hollywood type that walks the fine line between pimp and producer. One scene, which finds him snorting a line off Misty’s thigh, is pure, gleeful provocation.

	Rock’s entire ensemble is superb. Anna Kendrick gives her sharpest turn since “Up in the Air” as Misty’s best friend, a fellow actress drawn to Black men even as she dates the family-approved white ones. Topher Grace plays Misty’s talent agent, forced to deliver the hard truths about her erratic behavior. Rock casts himself as Jordan Green, a Hollywood director who knew Misty at her peak. Colleen Camp has a small, sly role, her second A24 film this year after “Club Kid.” Anthony Anderson plays a police officer, whose deadened delivery drives  the film toward some of its most uncomfortable scenes.

	“Misty Green” has plenty of laughs, but it curdles by the end — à la “Requiem for a Dream” — with scenes that drag Misty into the darkest depths of the business. 

	Nonetheless, Rock is building toward something less comfortable than a takedown of Hollywood vanity. The film is ultimately about is redemption and an examination of mental illness — and how thoroughly the country has failed to fund it, understand it or train anyone, its police most of all, to meet it. Anderson’s cop and Kaluuya’s brother are two ends of the same failure, and the movie sits in the space between them.

	For the upcoming Oscar race, Eleazar is a top-tier best actress contender in waiting. Kaluuya belongs in the supporting conversation on the strength of a single scene. And Rock, long underrated behind the camera since “Top Five,” has finally made the movie that earns his name a place in the screenplay and directing chatter.

	“Misty Green” opens in U.S. theaters on Oct. 9.
